The article defines computational functionalism more precisely than "the mind is what the brain computes" — it's the claim that implementing the right kind of computation is *sufficient* for consciousness to arise, whatever the hardware it runs on [spya-wepmnr]. That "sufficient" part matters: the whole essay hinges on treating this as an assumption, not a proven fact, since "the very idea of conscious AI rests on" it [spya-wepmnr].

Their answer does capture the substrate-independence piece — that the same "software" could be conscious on any suitable "hardware" — since Turing computation is described as "substrate independent: it does not depend on any particular material basis" [spya-dfujdu]. But the essay's central argument doesn't just note this assumption, it spends most of its length attacking it: brains aren't computers in the relevant sense, other non-computational dynamics may matter, life itself may be necessary for consciousness, and simulating something isn't the same as instantiating it [spya-cv97j7]. So the piece "matters for the whole essay" specifically because Seth is trying to show this assumption is likely false, which would mean "real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with" [spya-wepmnr] — worth adding to round out why the term is load-bearing for everything that follows.
items.context:
Q: What is 'computational functionalism' and why does it matter for the whole essay?
Reader's answer: It's the idea that the mind is basically what the brain computes, so the right software could be conscious on any hardware.

items.text:
The article's objection is different from this. Seth's point is not about verifying whether the person still feels the same — it's that the thought experiment assumes you *can* build a silicon neuron that functions exactly like a biological one, and he argues this is impossible in the first place. Some neurons fire spikes simply to clear metabolic waste products, and matching that would require inventing a whole silicon-based metabolism, "which just isn't the kind of thing silicon is suitable for" [spya-un9fjn]. Because a perfect functional replacement can't be built, "the argument fails at its first hurdle, given the impossibility of replacing any part of the brain with a perfect silicon equivalent" [spya-ahtr6e] — the flaw is in the premise, not in our ability to verify the outcome.

If you want to look again, the relevant passage is the section on the "neural replacement" thought experiment associated with Chalmers, right after the discussion of neurons that fire to clear waste products.
items.context:
Q: Why does Seth think the popular 'neural replacement' thought experiment fails to prove consciousness is substrate-independent?
Reader's answer: Because nobody could ever tell whether the person still felt the same after their neurons were swapped — you'd have to take their word for it.

items.text:
The storm example is right there in the piece — "A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything wet" [spya-npjt4j] — and it captures the core of the analogy well.

But the article stops short of the flat conclusion "can never be conscious." Seth's actual claim is conditional: a simulated brain gives rise to consciousness "only if consciousness is a matter of computation" — the whole point being that whether simulation could instantiate consciousness depends on whether computational functionalism is true, a question he treats as open in this specific argument, even though he argues elsewhere that functionalism is probably wrong. As he puts it, "a computational simulation of X does not bring X into being — does not instantiate X — unless X is a computational process (specifically, an algorithm) itself" [spya-npjt4j]. So the "simulation is not instantiation" point itself is meant as a general logical point (simulating X doesn't automatically produce X), separate from his separate case that brains likely aren't computers in the relevant sense.
items.context:
Q: What does Seth mean when he says 'simulation is not instantiation'?
Reader's answer: A simulation of a storm doesn't make anything wet, so a simulated brain can never be conscious.
